name: ScrollSnap
src_typeComment: Drop on the same GameObject as a ScrollRect whose Content uses a Horizontal or Vertical Layout Group with evenly-sized items. Dragging works exactly like a normal ScrollRect; releasing the drag eases to the nearest item automatically.

src_serialized.name: horizontal
src_serialized.tooltip: If true, snaps along the horizontal axis; otherwise vertical.

src_serialized.name: snapSpeed
src_serialized.tooltip: How quickly the scroll eases into the snapped position.

src_members.sig: public int ItemCount => scrollRect != null ? scrollRect.content.childCount : 0
src_members.name: ItemCount
src_members.comment: For anything that wants to know the page count without reaching into the ScrollRect itself — e.g. Toolkit.UI.PaginationDots.BindToScrollSnap().

src_members.sig: public void OnBeginDrag(PointerEventData eventData) => isSnapping = false
src_members.name: OnBeginDrag
src_members.comment: Without this, grabbing the scroll again mid-snap would leave LateUpdate still forcibly animating toward the old target every frame, fighting the user's new drag input.

src_members.name: SnapTo
src_members.comment: Call this directly for a "next/previous" button instead of dragging.

src_members.name: ComputeCenteredNormalizedPosition
src_members.comment: Centres the chosen item in the VIEWPORT.  The old version was `index / (itemCount - 1)`, which only centres an item when the viewport is exactly one item wide. With a viewport several items across it just distributes items along the scroll range, so the selected one lands wherever it happens to fall — the "does not snap the selected to middle" bug. The correct mapping accounts for the fact that normalized scroll 0..1 spans (content - viewport), not the whole content: take the item's own centre, subtract half a viewport to put it in the middle, then divide by the actual scrollable distance.

src_members.name: GetNearestItemIndex
src_members.comment: Finds the item whose centre is closest to the VIEWPORT's centre, by measuring actual positions rather than inverting the old normalized-position approximation — which, like SnapTo, only lined up when the viewport was exactly one item wide, so releasing a drag could pick a neighbour of the item actually under the middle.
